1.	Have any circular orders been issued by the Post Office Department, dated since February 18, 1954, advising letter carriers as to arrangements for annual leaves following the institution of the five-day 40-hour week?
2.	If so, how many of such circular orders have been issued, what are their numbers, and what were their dates of issue?
3.	What are the terms of such orders in relation to the arrangements for annual leaves for letter carriers?
4.	Did a subsequent order alter the terms of an earlier order? If so, in what respect?
5.	Do the terms of the latest order alter the established practice of annual leaves for letter carriers being arranged on the basis of seniority?
Questions
6.	If so, have protests been received against any such change?
7.	From whom?
8.	Has consideration been given to such protests? If so, what is the result of such consideration?
9.	Will the practice of annual leaves for letter carriers being arranged on the basis of seniority be reinstated?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Postmaster General
speechtext:
1 to 9.
To ensure the successful application of the five-day 40-hour week certain modifications of previous practices are essential. These changes are not derogatory to the general principle of the selection of annual leave by seniority in length of service.
The adoption of the rotation scheme whereby supervisory carriers relieve men on each of several walks in turn, from a standpoint of practical application, necessitates annual leave being taken within groups of 12 or 13 employees.
Two circular orders were issued; the first OBPS 299 of the 19th February outlining the application of annual leave on a basis of seniority within the group without regard to rank; the second OBPS 299D of the 26th February modifies the first and recognizes the supervisory rank of the supervisory letter carriers, indicating that seniority would be arranged first on a basis of rank and then the remainder of the employees on the basis of length of service.
Protests have been received from the national office of the federated association of letter carriers and also from several individual branches protesting against the supervisory class being given a choice of annual leave ahead of those letter carriers who wish to deliver on a single walk only and who do not wish to apply for or accept supervisory responsibilities.
Consideration is being given to this protest, and if it is possible to adopt the absolute rule of seniority within the groups that will be done. However, the basic requirement is that the interests of the public service must predominate.
Information so far received indicates that to give effect to the five-day week on April 1, 1954, it may be necessary to grant the holiday choice privilege to supervisory letter carriers at least at certain offices.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 376, to amend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act.
Does the minister intend to make a statement on second reading?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have nothing further to add to the statement I made on the resolution.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Will the minister be kind enough to wait until hon. members who have duties to perform outside the house leave their seats?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
The bill before us proposes to extend emergency gold mining assistance for the year 1954. Several hon. members asked questions during the debate on the resolution and I would prefer to wait until we reach the committee stage before answering those questions. However, there was one question in particular which perhaps I should answer at this time. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) asked if a mine benefited under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act during a strike. In calculating emergency gold mining assistance payments to a mine, two factors have to be considered:	first, the rate of assistance,
and secondly, the number of ounces produced which made that mine eligible for assistance. It is obvious that if there is no production there can be no gold eligible for assistance and therefore no payments during that period. Administrative or overhead costs, or anything which is normally considered an overhead cost, are not eligible for gold mining assistance payments during the period of a strike. In other words, a mine cannot benefit in any way whatsoever from the gold mining assistance during the period of a strike. The rate of assistance is calculated on the cost of production, assuming that there was a full year's operation. That rate is applied only to the assistance ounces eligible. When there is no production, there is no gold eligible for assistance.

Mr. Speaker, I see no reason why this bill should be unduly held up at this moment. However, I just wanted to answer certain statements which were put on the record by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) with regard to the earnings of gold mining companies. Of the 53 straight gold mines which are at present in production, the average yield is rather less than per cent on the present price of the stock. May I say that that yield is considerably under the yield of any group of manufacturing stocks or that on stocks of any other producers of primary products. As to dividends paid, for the straight gold mines in 1953-that is the 53 straight gold mines which were producing-the average dividend was 15 cents. If one excluded the McIntyre mine

which is now more of an investment trust than a gold producer, the average dividend would fall to 9 cents. I merely wanted to put these facts on the record in order to show that today the gold mining industry is not making profits and is virtually scraping the bottom of the barrel.
As to wages, while the wages paid in the straight gold mining industry are less than those paid in the base metal mines, nevertheless they compare favourably with and are very much higher than the average of industrial wages across Canada. I have the statistics in front of me but I will not burden the house by putting them on the record. However, they are here in the dominion bureau of statistics' statistical review and in the Labour Review.
There is one other comment I should like to make with regard to wages in the gold camps and it is this. The cost of living in the settled camps is considerably lower than that in places such as Sudbury or the industrial centres of southern Ontario and industrial Quebec. Rents are lower. The cost of living generally is lower. Hence, after the cost of living has been taken out, the balance position of the gold miner at the end of the month is, I submit, little if at all inferior to that of the worker in any other industry in Canada.
I think that is all I wish to say on the bill now, Mr. Speaker. As I said yesterday, we support it. I will not repeat anything I said yesterday on the matter. I merely wanted to correct a statement which I believe can be shown to be untrue.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to delay the passage of this bill. When speaking earlier on this subject I made it clear that we would support this bill. There are, however, certain things that we think should be taken into consideration at this time.
When speaking on the resolution yesterday I emphasized the fact that among those interested in the gold mines in the north there was a growing demand for the setting up of a commission or a special committee to consider the present status of the gold mining industry. As I indicated then, there is a great deal of confusion with regard to that status. The mine owners have certainly succeeded in selling to the government, to the press and to the Conservative party the idea that gold mining is a depressed industry at the present time. The mine owners succeeded in persuading the public, through the press, that last winter they could not afford to pay the increased wages asked for by the miners nor to introduce shorter hours for the work-week which is now a 48-hour
Gold Mining
week, notwithstanding the fact that six conciliation boards under the chairmanship of Mr. Eric Taylor, Judge Lane, Judge Fuller and Professor Curtis, after examining the financial statements of these mines, had all found that, in their opinion, the mines could afford to grant the increase in wages asked for and a shorter work-week, and so recommended in their report.
There is also some confusion as to whether or not this act is fulfilling the purpose for which it was intended. In the report on the administration of the act, we are told this: The Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act of 1948 was primarily designed to assist the high cost or marginal gold mines to continue operations throughout the difficult post-war period.
There is a question whether the act as it stands at present, and with the present regulations, meets that need. There is some doubt as to the extent to which the public funds paid to the gold mines does that. This year these funds will probably amount to about $13 million. From a return handed down, I gather there is another cost of approximately $65,000, that being the cost of administering the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act to the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and the Department of Finance. As handed down in the return in my name, the total cost of administering this act in 1953 would be approximately $65,000.
With so much public money going into the industry, it is certainly relevant to ask whether the miners and the communities affected are receiving the benefits from this act or whether the benefits of this public money are being siphoned off in profits to directors, shareholders and mining stock speculators. Charges have been made and evidence has been given before conciliation boards to the effect that neither the miners nor the communities have benefited from the funds which the federal government has provided. That is one reason why I think there should be a more thorough investigation of the whole situation.
The act purports to exist for the purpose of assisting high-cost or marginal gold mines to continue operation. Actually, in 1952, of the $10,359,000 paid in gold subsidies $1,390,000 went to two mines, Hollinger and McIntyre. In that year sixty-one mines applied for subsidies. Approximately $9 million was divided among the remaining fifty-nine, whereas the lion's share of the subsidies certainly went to the two largest gold mines.
The question arises whether or not these mines were deliberately budgeting for a deficit on their operations in order to take the fullest possible advantage of the subsidies paid by the federal government. There

Gold Mining
is some evidence from their reports that unusual quantities of low grade ore were used with the higher grades in order to maintain minimum production from the ores mined so that the greatest possible benefits could be derived from the subsidies. There are other equally important questions which I think can only be solved by a thorough-going investigation of the whole gold mining industry in relation to the general economy of the country. I would urge the minister to take that into consideration.
I was very happy to hear from the minister that no subsidy could possibly be paid for gold that was not produced and that the mines could not benefit from the subsidy while they were on strike. I want to point out to the minister my reason for believing that such was possible by referring to section 6(1) (d) of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act which provides as follows:
. . . where the operation of a mine is suspended during part of a designated year for a reason specified in the regulations . . . payments may be made ... in such amount as would have been payable ... if the mine had been in normal operation throughout the designated year . . .
Then I turn to regulation 15 of order in council P.C. 2664 of June 11, 1948. This regulation includes suspension of operation by strike and provides in part as follows:
. . . assistance payments may be made for the gold actually produced during the year in such amount as would have been payable in respect of that gold if the operation of the mine had not been suspended . . .
Those who have given considerable study to that regulation, including some auditors, have reached the conclusion that it would appear that if operations were suspended for thirty days only the period of thirty days would be treated as if there had been no suspension, but where suspension of operations is more than thirty days then it would seem that at least part of the cost to the company of suspension of operations is included in the costs for the purpose of determining the assistance payable under the act.
I have before me sessional paper 78-B which purports to be a copy of the report made by the cost inspection and audit division of the office of the comptroller of the treasury with respect to Hollinger for the year 1951 during which year the mine was on strike for fifty-eight days. I find that the production for the designated year 1951 was 241,429.898 fine ounces. I also find that the production for the designated year 1951, if the mine had not suspended operations, works out by the application of the formula to 287,004.167 fine ounces, which is about 46,000 more than the number of ounces actually produced. Then I find that in working out the assistance

ounces, if the mine had not suspended operations, the figure 287,004.167 is used instead of the figure of 241,000, which was the actual production for that year.
From that return it would appear that in that particular case some advantage accrued to the mine for the period of fifty-eight days during which it was closed down. I am quite sure that everyone interested will be very happy to have the public assurance of the minister that mines cannot profit from this act when they are on strike. I would point out to the minister that that is fair. Under the Unemployment Insurance Act no employee may collect unemployment insurance while his firm is on strike, and it is only fair that the same rule should apply to employers and that they should not be able to benefit in any way from federal revenues by reason of the fact that they are on strike.
I would ask the minister to have his department look over that return, sessional paper No. 78-B, entitled "Cost Inspection and Audit Division, Office of the Comptroller of the Treasury," dated August 14, 1952, in which the number of assistance ounces was calculated as I have indicated. It may be that the minister can show me from that calculation that Hollinger did not benefit in any way from those fifty-eight days. I will admit that the formula is a very complicated one, and it would take someone as conversant with it as the minister himself to be able to tell us whether or not that is true.

I
only want to speak for a few minutes, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) yesterday and today put very well the point of view of this group, and the questions in which we are particularly interested. I do not see, therefore, any particular reason for repeating his explanation and his arguments.
There are many miners in British Columbia interested in this legislation. As a consequence representatives of the international union of mine, mill and smelter workers came to Ottawa and made representations on behalf of their members in Canada to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham), the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), and the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair). I may say that union has represented the hard-rock miners in British Columbia since 1896, so it has had considerable experience with the problem of miners and particularly with those of the gold mining industry.
When in Ottawa the union representatives presented a brief to the ministers in question, and I understand they received a courteous and careful hearing. As a result of their

experience they made certain representations. I am not going to deal with the brief at length but I should like to read the final recommendation from the statement and proposals adopted by the sixth Canadian convention of the international union of mine, mill and smelter workers, for submission to the government of Canada. The proposal reads, and I support it:
Finally, we urge that a federal inquiry be undertaken into the gold mining industry in Canada, with the right of all interested parties to appear before the inquiry board, to give evidence and make proposals to assist the industry and for the advantage of the workers employed in it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to make this point. It is obvious from the situation that has developed in the gold mining industry in recent years, and it is obvious from the minister's remarks that the industry is not in the condition today that the government expected it to be in when this measure of assistance was first introduced. There is a great deal of uncertainty. The workers in the industry are not satisfied with their conditions. They have no sense of security. I should like the minister, when he concludes this debate, to give consideration to this recommendation, which I believe was previously mentioned by the hon. member for York South. It seems to me to be a sound recommendation. I should like the minister to inform the house if he would recommend to his colleagues that an inquiry into the gold industry in Canada be undertaken by the federal government, in view of the situation illustrated by recent events, this debate, and by the remarks of the minister upon introducing the bill from year to year when renewal of the measure was under consideration by the house.

The gold mining industry would be in a very different position today were the price of its product in relation to the prices of other commodities comparable to the prices which prevailed before the second world war. Unfortunately, it is the other way around. The price of gold was kept down to the 1934 basis of $35 in United States currency and the cost of production has gone up.
In view of this, it must be realized that the industry has no other alternative but to accept government assistance, even if this assistance is short of compensating for the rise in production costs. An advance in the price of gold is the only permanent solution to the problem of the gold mines, but as Canada is not the largest producer or seller of the precious metal we cannot dictate the price or influence the buyers by refusing to sell. We are faced with this problem, that
Gold Mining
the price of gold can only be raised by joint international action for which the initiative rests with the United States.
Canada would certainly stand to gain from an increase in the official price of gold. Not only would a higher price be of direct benefit to the Canadian gold producers and those dependent upon them, but by increasing the United States dollar value of gold the official reserve held outside the United States would ease some of the exchange difficulties and lead to an increase in Canadian export. However, the price of gold is not something that our government alone has the power to determine. The predominant position of the United States, as the world's largest holder and buyer of gold, means that the value the United States government places on gold in terms of its own currency is the official world price. Only lately our influential friends to the south have again stated that the price should stay at $35 in United States currency, and that is all there is to it.
We are all aware that the production and sale of gold is of great importance to the Canadian economy. Until there is an increase in the price, we must agree that the government will have to continue to assist the industry. Let us review what has happened to the gold mining industry in Canada during the past years, and more particularly since 1948 when the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act came into force. Let us see if the government has so badly invested the Canadian taxpayers' money, if the gold producers have abused the assistance received, and if the miners and other people dependent on the industry have not benefited by it.
It is not my intention to take the time of the house to review the causes for the seriously handicapped operations of the gold mining industry in Canada since the early years of world war II. However, let me say that during those years the gold producers were sharply restricted in supplies, equipment and manpower. The volume and dollar value of production were reduced to practically one-half by the end of the war. During the years immediately following the end of the war rapidly mounting costs pressing against the ceiling of a fixed price for gold brought the industry to a precarious position. The figures published by the dominion bureau of statistics show that the operating costs of Canadian gold mines have risen by 35 per cent during the period between the year 1941, when the price of gold was $38.50 an ounce, and the year 1948 when the price of gold was $35 an ounce. Since 1948, when cost aid was instituted, the upward trend of costs has been particularly marked. During the period between 1948 and 1951 wages

Gold Mining
rose 32-3 per cent, costs of supplies 34-7 per cent and freight costs close to 50 per cent. Those three items of cost together constitute 84 per cent of the total cost of operation of the average gold mine.
After 1951 the upward trend has continued, and we can say that during the past eight years the gold mines have been waging a hard battle. They have tried to maintain production in the face of rising costs, with no offsetting increase in the price of gold. The most recent report published by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys shows that for the year 1952, of the 56 lode gold mines which were in receipt of cost aid, thirty-five are reported as having costs in excess of $35 an ounce, sixteen are reported as having costs in excess of $30 an ounce, and only five are reported as having costs between $25 and $30 an ounce.
From this it will be realized that the majority of the gold mines would be unable to maintain production at the current price of gold, without assistance; and that sixteen pther mines are in a precarious position, where costs and revenue are about in balance. In that same report which I have just mentioned we find that from 1948 to 1951 inclusive at least 50 per cent of the gold mines in receipt of cost aid have been reported as having costs in excess of $35 an ounce.
To alleviate the disastrous effect which the Canadian gold mining industry and the communities dependent upon it were suffering, as a result of the closing vise of mounting costs against a fixed price, the government introduced in 1948 this legislation, which we now hope will be extended to the end of 1954.
As previously mentioned, the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was sanctioned in 1948, and it was to stay in force for three years. In 1951, 1952 and 1953 it was extended and amended and each time a bill was introduced in the house to this effect there was very little or no opposition. This time it looks to be the same thing; but there are insinuations that there has been abuse of this assistance, that it did not benefit the miners and communities dependent upon the industry.
Before I present some facts which will prove that the assistance provided by the government did benefit the miners and mining communities, I wish to go back to the debate which took place in 1948 during the second reading of the bill respecting emergency payments to assist in meeting increased costs of production of gold. I wish to refer to some of the remarks made at that time by the leader of the C.C.F. party. This is very important, Mr. Speaker, because at that time

the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) did not oppose the measure which was then before the house; but he made certain observations and did insist that the said measure was acceptable only under certain conditions.
As reported at page 2675 of Hansard for April 6, 1948, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar had this to say:
I think this can be justified only if we accept certain considerations which should be fundamental to the granting of any subsidy of this kind, namely that the subsidy should not be used for the profit of the owners of the mines but should be granted only if we have not merely an understanding but a definite undertaking that the men engaged in the mining industry are paid decent and sufficient wages and work and live under decent and proper conditions.
And later the hon. member had this to say:
May I say to the minister I have been told that when the representatives of the unions discussed this matter on one occasion with one of the ministers, I believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), he was willing to accept the suggestion that some sixty per cent of the grants made by the government under a measure such as this should be used for the improvement of conditions of labour and of health, and the rates of pay of the men engaged in the industry.
And again:
In any event, whatever we do in matters of this kind should be done with the distinct understanding, and, as I said, on the distinct undertaking, that a proper proportion of whatever aid is given shall be used for the improvement of conditions among those who risk life and limb and health in the mining of gold.
From what I have just cited, I suppose I am right in saying that the leader of the C.C.F. party gave his approval of the measure then before the house subject to certain conditions: First, that the men engaged in the mining industry were to be paid decent and sufficient wages; and second, that they were to work and live under decent and proper conditions. And I presume that I am right also in saying that it was proposed to accept the suggestion that some sixty per cent of the assistance to be granted by the government was to be used to this effect.
Well, Mr. Speaker, after what was said in 1948, it is appropriate that the house be informed for what purpose the assistance provided to the Canadian gold mines by the government under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was used.
First of all, what portion of the assistance went to pay increases in wages and salaries? In 1947, the average annual wage of a miner in a Canadian gold mine was $2,277. The corresponding figure for 1948 was $2,537, an increase of 11-4 per cent. For 1949, the average wage was $2,650, an increase of 16-4 per cent over 1947. In 1950, the average wage

of a miner was $2,765, an increase of 21-3 per cent over 1947. And in 1951, the average wage was $3,013, an increase of 32-3 per cent over 1947.
During the period for which figures are available from the dominion bureau of statistics, that is from 1948 to 1951 inclusive, we find that the total increase in wages and salaries paid by the gold producers is equivalent to 99-7 per cent of the total assistance paid by the government.
That is substantially more than 60 per cent. The total assistance paid to the industry during that period amounted to $41,404,000, while the increase in wages and salaries totalled $41,281,302. During the same period the industry paid $26,666,000 in federal, provincial and municipal taxes, which alone represents 64 [DOT] 4 per cent of the total assistance received by the gold mines.
During that same period of four years between 1948 and 1951 the total amount of wages and salaries paid by the lode gold mining industry amounted to $254,082,000. The aggregate cost of supplies, plant, equipment, buildings and machinery amounted to $220 million. Those figures are interesting and it is most important that we take them into consideration.
While wages and supplies and freight are the principal items of costs in operating gold mines, they are by no means the only factors which contribute to increase costs of operation.
In addition account has to be taken of improved health and welfare services, increased rates of workmen's compensation, and many other items which in total amount to substantial sums.
And we must be reminded of this. The gold mining industry is the only industry which has to absorb these increases into the costs of operation without being able to pass on to consumers any portion of such increased costs.
Now as to the working and living conditions in the gold mines and in the communities. Are they as bad as some people try to make us believe they are? Are the gold producers so uninterested in the welfare of their employees as to do nothing about it? Are they trying to evade municipal and school taxes as we are being told?
The answers to those questions can be found in safety records and annual municipal reports which are available to whoever wants to look at them. If one looks at these reports he will find that the industry has done everything possible to improve health and welfare services in its operation and that it has
Gold Mining
co-operated in the best possible manner with municipal authorities to improve living conditions in the mining communities.
The mining producers across Canada are fully conscious of the importance of safe workings in the mines. They know very well that safe mines enjoy better labour relations with their employees. And in this respect the Canadian gold mines are not lagging behind, as you will be able to note from the following.
The Canada-wide contest sponsored by the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy, under which the John T. Ryan trophies are awarded annually to the mine in Canada with the lowest compensable accident record, resulted in a most creditable way for the Ontario and Quebec gold mines during the last five years.
In 1948 the winner of the trophy with the best safety record of all the metal mines in Canada was the Toburn Gold Mines of the Kirkland Lake district. In 1949 the trophy was awarded to Matachewan Consolidated, another mine in Ontario. In 1950, the John T. Ryan trophy travelled across the interprovincial boundary to be awarded to Sigma Mines Limited in Val d'Or, Quebec. And in 1951 and 1952, Canadian Malartic Gold Mines Limited won the John T. Ryan award for safety. This gold mine, which is located in my home town, had not one single compensable accident during 1952. This record is probably the best in Canadian mining history. What an extraordinary record for an industry where, according to some people, working conditions are supposed to be so bad.
Mr. Speaker, our gold miners do their jobs with care and ability; they are safety conscious, and in this respect they are encouraged and seconded by those in charge of management. What I have just said should be sufficient to show that, as far as good working conditions are concerned, the gold mines and the miners are, if anything, showing the way to many other industries.
Now as regards this question of dividends which are paid quarterly, semi-annually or annually by the gold mines. What about this famous question? Is it a crime for an industry to pay a dividend? What about the shareholders? Are they to forgo the revenues which are rightly due to them? The answers to these questions are as follows.
First of all the net revenues of all the gold mines are at a very low ebb. The gold mines which did not alter their dividend rates are those which are not in receipt of cost aid. Or whatever dividends are being paid these days by most of the gold mines are taken from surplus earned from other

Gold Mining
sources than their actual operations. Others are squeezing their dividends from accumulated surplus earned during the good years before the second world war. And many other gold mines are not paying any dividends at all. How long they will be able to continue to do that, we do not know. And for how long will they be able to ask their shareholders to be patient? They certainly cannot tell them that this is the new way of operating a business.
From 1948 to 1952 inclusive, out of 27 Quebec gold mines which received assistance from the government 15 never paid any dividends. Five others paid less than $230,000 each during those five years. The six remaining gold mines paid dividends on a reduced rate and it is important to note that during that same period those six gold mines paid more than $27,000 in increased wages alone, over and above what they received in assistance from the government.
The shareholders in the Canadian gold mining industry are many thousands and the great majority of them are small shareholders. We must keep that in mind, and I will go as far as to say that the government, both in its role of tax collector and in its role of representative of the broader interests of all Canadians, has the responsibility to hang on to the gold mining industry; and hanging on means helping the shareholders, the employees, the small property owners, the farmers and the business people dependent on gold mining to hang on.
I also wish to remind hon. members that the gold mining industry, important as it is, is only one branch of the metal mining industry of this country which gives employment to some 130,000 men who in turn are the supporters of more than 500,000 people. So in trying to establish some comparison between the assistance allocated to the gold mines and that which is granted to other key industries, it would only be fair to keep those figures in mind.
The Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act is plain evidence of the government's recognition of the importance of the gold mining industry in the national economy. It is the intention of the government to ensure, so far as lies in its power, the condition under which the industry may have not only continuity of operation but the possibility and hope of extensive development.
The welfare of the gold mining communities has always been regarded by the government as of very great importance. For this I wish to express my thanks. The fact that this government has definitely come forward with the present legislation is encouraging 
to the industry and to the residents of the gold mining communities. We are all very thankful.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say this. Let us consider this question calmly, and let us not forget that the closing down of the industry would mean the uprooting of families, the abandonment of towns which have been built at the cost of many millions of dollars and which are complete with all the facilities of modern living. There are 30 such mining communities across the country and they are providing ready and important markets for farm and lumber products, manufactured commodities and many other kinds of supplies.
This great wealth and economic activity would be jeopardized by the closing down of the gold mines, and it is up to this parliament to safeguard them. In discussing this bill we have to keep these facts in mind, and if we do I believe this legislation will meet with the approval of all hon. members.

Mr. Speaker, in supporting this bill I believe I should first correct some of the statements made and impressions left by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) when he spoke in this house on November 20, yesterday, and again today. You will recall that he stated at that time that he was qualified to speak on this subject as he had worked at every process in gold mines from mucking to milling. It must have been a long, long time ago. It is very evident to me that he has no appreciation whatever of the seriousness of the problem facing the gold mining industry in Canada today.
The hon. member professes to be gravely concerned with the plight of the workers and the communities, but he proceeds to do as much harm as possible to the industry on which they are all, almost solely, dependent. Many of his remarks were completely unwarranted, and many were divorced from fact, as will be shown by the information I propose to place before hon. members today, and information which has already been placed on record by other speakers.
I believe it might be well if I dealt with the hon. member's statement as reported at page 485 of Hansard in which he said:
What precautions are taken by the government to ensure that these mines are not deliberately keeping their mill heads low in order to mill their low-grade ore while the government subsidy is available, and sealing off their higher grade ore until such time as they can get a higher price for gold or a higher subsidy from this government? I have met miners in northern Ontario who told me their job has been to seal off high-grade ore whenever it was discovered and to keep it for future

development, while the low-grade ore was fed to the mill and emergency gold mining assistance used in order to pay for part of the cost of that milling.
It will be noted that this hon. member and certain other people quoted in the press to the same effect have not named one single mine. However, I would ignore that statement because to those of us who are really familiar with gold mining it is a ridiculous statement, though just a little complicated to answer because the act itself is not readily understandable unless you sit down and study it.
When this statement was made I was a little amused because I immediately had a vision of men running around underground with a bucketful of cement and a trowel and covering up high-grade gold nuggets. Then I realized it is possible that people might believe such a statement. I am therefore going to answer it in such a way that I hope no one could possibly believe it again.
One of the saddest things about the gold mining industry is the fact that once you have mined in a specific area and abandon it you cannot ever go back and mine in that same area again. It is much too dangerous and in a period such as this when costs are so high, and the price of gold is so low, every day in every gold mine in Canada it is necessary to by-pass ore, or what is known as waste rock, because you cannot economically mine it, though there is a substantial amount of gold in it. If the price of gold were commensurate with our dollar today it would be good ore rather than waste rock, and since there is not too much gold in the world, it is a pity we have to lose it. However, that cannot be helped.
Mining is a very difficult engineering problem. It takes long-term planning and it is essential that a mine management arrange the digging out of the proven ore bodies underground in such a manner that they maintain a constant millhead. In other words, they endeavour to send up from underground each day the kind of ore which will have approximately, when it is all mixed together, the same amount of gold; otherwise they would have to change their solutions, and do all kinds of complicated things that would run up costs. It is not a question of grabbing it from here today and from there tomorrow. Furthermore, the act is drawn in such a manner that it would not be advantageous to leave high-grade ore and mill low-grade ore. Under the act assistance is based on two factors, the cost of production and the number of ounces produced. The cost of production for the purpose of the act is defined as "the cost incurred by the operator properly attributable to the gold produced from a
Gold Mining
mine during that particular year". The number of ounces on which the subsidy is paid is defined as the number of ounces by which the number produced from the mine and sold in the designated year exceeded one-half of the number of the ounces produced from the mine in the base year, or to one-half of the number of ounces produced and sold in the designated year, whichever is the greater.
Suppose we assume that any mine management would deliberately leave high-grade ore in the ground and mine only low-grade ore in order to run up costs and thereby receive a larger subsidy, as suggested by the hon. member. Just what would be the net result to the shareholders of the mine? The higher subsidy is based on the actual proven costs of production of an ounce of gold. It must be obvious to anyone that if you bring up two tons of rock out of the ground and treat it to obtain one ounce of gold, where formerly you brought up one ton to get one ounce of gold, then your expenses will be doubled. How could you have any net gain by receiving a slightly larger subsidy per ounce, especially when the subsidy does not begin to compensate for all of the increased costs, and is only paid on a part of the total ounces produced in any specific mine?
Let me give hon. members a concrete example of what would actually happen to a specific mine if it did what is suggested by the hon. member for York South, or if their present grade of ore petered out. I take for this example the Kirkland Lake Gold Mining Company Limited-that is one in my own community-and I use their actual experience in 1952. During this year they produced 44,828 ounces of gold. Their costs of production were $36.02 per ounce. They received approximately $177,000 in assistance. Their profit, before taxes, was approximately $125,800. What would happen if they deliberately or otherwise reduced their grade of ore by as little as 5 per cent? Their costs would be greater per ounce recovered so their assistance would increase slightly. If this had actually been the case, they would have received $6,061 more in subsidy. But do not forget the fact that the grade is decreased by 5 per cent, so they would have 2,240 fewer ounces to sell. Therefore on their total income for the year they would actually lose $70,817 by reducing the grade just by 5 per cent. In other words, their profit for the year, before taxes, would become $54,987 instead of approximately $125,000 as it actually was. This with only a 5 per cent reduction in the grade of ore.
I want to carry this idea just one step further. If the grade were reduced by 10 per cent, the cost of producing an ounce of gold

Gold Mining
would have been increased by $4 an ounce and the subsidy would have been increased by $10,000; but the company would have had a net loss of income for the year of $143,767 by reason of the 10 per cent lower grade. So instead of making approximately $125,000 profit before taxes, as they did, they would have actually been in the red by $17,963 on the year's operation.
The only object in mining is to obtain a profit from a given body of ore, and the main problem in achieving this purpose are keeping costs down and the grade up. The government officials responsible for the drafting of this act should be complimented.- At first glance it appears to be complicated, but in operation it has proved to be most adequate to assure sound administration and fair distribution of the subsidy.
One of the major problems facing all but a few of the gold mines is to find enough high-grade ore in order to continue operations at all under existing circumstances.
On the same subject of subsidy paid to the industry the hon. member inferred, at page 487 of Hansard, that the mines could receive the maximum cost aid on all of the gold produced, which for 1953 was $13.50 per ounce, making a total per ounce that the mines would receive of $48.50. He cites the case of one mine-listed in this blue report from the department-which received the maximum for 1952. But he failed to mention that that was a new mine and had operated for only a portion of the year. This is provided for in the act. But all other mines receive the subsidy on only a portion of their production, as I have just explained. In other words, a mine in its first year of operation receives subsidy on its entire production for that year only; thereafter it receives subsidy on 50 per cent of its next year's production or 50 per cent of the previous year's production, whichever is the greater. This should have been known to the hon. member as he was at the time quoting from the report of the administration of the act.
One who is really interested in the subsidy paid to Canadian lode gold mines on the total ounces produced has but to read the averages published in the same report at pages 10 to 12. They are as follows:
1948		$3-27
1949		 3-42
1950		 2-33
1951		 3 29
1952		 3-91
That figure of $3.91, however, may be greater when the full returns are in. This is the average subsidy to the industry when the total gold produced by the lode mines receiving subsidy is taken into consideration. This

is a completely different picture from that inferred by the hon. member for York South.
During this five-year period the gold mines suffered a loss of approximately $4.23 per ounce of gold produced, by reason of the appreciation in the Canadian dollar over the United States dollar. The costs of production still kept mounting during this period but the average subsidy paid per ounce did not even offset the drop in the price of the finished product.
It is of interest to note that there were only two new mines in all Canada in 1952 in receipt of subsidy, as shown in the report of the administration of the act. There were none in 1953. If the mines were "making a killing" as a union officer was quoted in the press as saying the other day, or if the statements made by the hon. member for York South have any logic, how do they account for the many mines that have been forced to close, or for the fact that there are no new gold mines being opened for the first time in many years?
In an effort to prove that this is not a depressed industry, as reported at page 487 of Hansard, the hon. member for York South refers to the profits paid by two mines out of all those in Canada, one of them being McIntyre, when it is well known that only a portion of their profits is earned from the current gold mining operation. As to the other one, Broulan Reef, he states specifically that this is one of the mines which received cost aid in 1952-and if I am not mistaken he stated that twice-and yet made a large profit. This is just not so. They did not receive one cent of cost aid in 1952. They are one of the lucky mines that ran into extremely high-grade ore and they were selling on the premium market, so-called, in 1952.
Citing the number of dollars profit made by any particular mine means little unless accompanied by the number of tons mined daily, the number of men employed, the number of shareholders and the amount of stock issued and, finally, the number of years that the mine had to operate before it showed any profit at all. As an example, one of the mines in my community operated for many years-I think it was almost 20-before it was in a position to make any profit whatever.
The other day I quoted some figures that bear repeating. An analysis of the gold mining industry in Ontario from 1941 to 1951 shows that 35 per cent have discontinued operations; 74 per cent of the profits of the industry have been wiped out; 40 per cent fewer men are employed. The picture would be worse today. In the face of these facts, how can anyone say that this is not a depressed industry?

Again, the decline of the industry, in spite of cost aid, is shown very clearly in the report of the administration of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. In 1948 there were 87 lode gold mines in receipt of cost aid; in 1952 there were only 56. There were 13 selling on the "premium market" in 1952 and one that had not filed a statement at the time the report was published, making 17 lode gold mines closed during this five-year period.
As a further item bearing on this point, I quote from a statistical summary of the Bank of Canada showing the net operating profits of a representative group of Canadian gold mines. They picked out the group; I did not. In 1940 the profits were $58-4 million. In 1950, ten years later, the profits were $18-5 million. Of course, in 1950 they were in receipt of cost aid.
From the Canadian Metal Mining Association I also have some figures showing the estimated handicap per ounce incurred by Ontario lode gold mines during the periods shown, and this excludes any increase in tax rates which have doubled since 1939. From 1939 to September 1952, increase in operating costs per ounce, $11.93; reduction in price received for gold, $4.90; estimated total handicap without increase in taxes, $16.83.
These are but some of the actual facts that prompted the government to introduce the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. The hon. member also made statements with respect to wages and the use of the subsidy. I must read hon. members what he said, as found at page 485 of Hansard of November 30. He said:
I am merely pointing out that if the government finds it necessary to subsidize the gold mines, then some measure must be taken to see that this benefit from the public treasury goes to the miners and the community, and is not all siphoned off in profits for shareholders and speculative stock buyers.
Again, he said, as found at page 487:
There has been no increase in wages in gold mining in Ontario and Quebec since 1951.
He also said:
Are we as custodians of the taxpayers' interests to stand idly by, or to sit idly by, while gold mine operators pass on all the cost aid they can possibly extract from this government to profits, with coldblooded, calculated indifference alike to miners and mining communities? I suggest that the basis on which cost aid is given be reviewed in order to make certain that miners as well as mine owners benefit from these federal subsidies.
The Labour Gazette shows that the annual average wages in Canadian gold mines were as follows: 1950, $2,765; 1951, $2,992 and 1952, $3,107. Ontario and Quebec between them produced 89 per cent of the total gold produced in Canada. Therefore I think it is conclusive from the figures that some increases must have been paid since 1951.
Gold Mining
But the following figures apply to Ontario alone and show that the statement with respect to no increase in Ontario is absolutely wrong. Furthermore, they prove conclusively that the statements made by hon. member for York South with respect to the subsidy being used to increase profits and none of it being used to increase the wages of the workers are entirely without foundation in fact-quite the contrary.
I should like to refer first to the Northern Miner and figures covering eleven mines in the Porcupine area. They show that during the period January 1, 1948, when the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act came into being, to the end of December, 1952, these eleven mines in the Porcupine area received almost $11J million in subsidy. But note this. For a slightly longer period, from January 1, 1948, into 1953 the amount paid out by these mines in increased wages was $16,365,000. Almost $5 million more was paid out in increased wages by these eleven mines in the Porcupine area. It is true that the $5 million does include the increase paid in 1953, but that did not amount to $5 million.
I have other figures that are better in that they cover the exact period. I have figures covering three mines in the Porcupine area, Dome, Delnite and Preston East Dome, for the identical period from January 1, 1948, to December 31, 1952. They received $3,425,205 in cost aid and paid out in wage increases during the same period $4,514,085. In other words, they paid out $1,088,000 more than the total subsidy they received. For my own camp, the Kirkland camp, I have figures for every single one of the mines still operating. Unfortunately several of them have had to close down. I have figures for Macassa, Kirkland Lake Gold, Sylvanite, Lake Shore, Wright-Hargreaves and Teck-Hughes. I can give individual figures if desired but otherwise I will give totals.
They received $3,471,759 in subsidies during those five years and paid out in wage increases during the same period $5,370,876, $1,899,000 more than they received in total subsidies. Of course where there were profits-and there is no point in a mine staying in business if there are no profits-they would not even receive the total subsidy because they have to pay taxes on it. I have given total figures and not what individual miners received. It cannot be said there were more men employed and therefore these millions I have told you about that were paid out in excess of the subsidies are accounted for because there were more men. The reverse is true. There were fewer men. The Ontario department of mines shows in a report that in 1941 there were 19,500 men

Gold Mining
employed in the gold mines of Ontario and that in 1952 there were 11,800 men employed. In other words, there were 7,700 fewer men in Ontario alone. Yet the hon. member says there is no depression in the industry.
Let me say one more word about wages. At the time the price of $35 per ounce was established it was adequate for the sound development of the mines and to pay top wages. The following figures are taken from the annual review of employment and payrolls, dominion bureau of statistics. Just yesterday the same hon. member said, as recorded at page 3033 of Hansard:
But never at any time in the history ol gold mining in this country have those who actually mine and mill the gold received their fair share of the wealth produced from the mines.
Hear, hear.

These figures show the average weekly earnings in gold mining and certain heavy manufacturing industries in 1939 and 1952. The other industries are iron and steel products, transportation equipment, non-ferrous metal products and electrical apparatus and supplies. In 1939 the gold mines of Canada paid $34.10 per week on the average. That is $6.86 a week more than the highest paid in any of the other four heavy industries referred to in the bureau of statistics report. That is why I say that when we did receive an adequate price top wages were paid. In 1952-I think this is very significant-we find that the gold mines *of Canada paid an average wage per week of $63.21, but we find that only one other heavy industry in the list paid any more. The non-ferrous metal products industry paid an average of $63.88 but the others paid less. Electrical apparatus and supplies paid $60.86. They have no difficulty with respect to the price of their finished products, nor do any of the others.
On the one hand the hon. member for York South claims that the gold mining industry is making enormous profits by reason of the subsidy, and on the other hand that they are leaving their high-grade ore in the ground. This just does not make sense, particularly when the increased wages alone since the act came into being have cost most of the mines more than the total subsidy each mine received. Such statements as those made by the hon. member for York South create a false impression and do not contribute to a full and sympathetic understanding of the problems of the gold mining industry and the thousands of Canadian pioneers and the communities almost solely dependent thereon, for whom he expresses such concern.

It is not generally understood that almost all gold mining municipalities would not exist if it were not for the mines. We cannot attract secondary industries for a variety of reasons, leaving us almost solely dependent on the one industry. These mining communities were literally hewn from the forest and rock. Our mortgages on our homes, if we can get them, and our municipal debentures are all for a shorter period because of the nature of our industry, and in the early days rates were very much higher than elsewhere in the country.
In a gold mining community the costs of sanitary facilities are excessive because we live in a cold climate. My own community, for instance, is built on solid rock, and you all know the cost of excavating rock as compared with soil. The cost of our fuel is greater up there. We are a very young part of the country, and in 1939 the birth rate at Kirkland Lake was the highest in Canada. This made it necessary for us to build schools every year, and you all know the cost of that. We were paying for everything at once. Our communities are very young, and we have to pay for schools, churches, sanitary facilities and so on, all at once and in a shorter period of time.
These things we accept as part of our way of life. You never hear us complain about them. We built these communities, and almost everything most of us own is invested there, our homes and our businesses. The owners of the mines are not a handful of wealthy men as some would lead us to believe. They comprise thousands of small investors, the miner himself, the butcher, the baker, the housewife and no doubt even some members of parliament. During the war our experienced gold miners enlisted in great numbers. Some were required in the base metal mines to increase the production of strategic metals. Our women continually produced more materials for the Red Cross than any other group in Canada.
Those things we did gladly, but what of today? What does the future hold? There is no simple answer to our problem except a much higher world price for our gold. This solution is beyond the control of any one country or government. If it is feasible, and in the national interest, I know this government will press strongly for such a solution. Canada has done much to keep the gold mining industry alive through the establishment of emergency gold mining assistance. By the terms of the bill now before us, the government proposes to continue that assistance for another year. If disaster is not to overtake our gold mining communities from one side of Canada to the other, adequate

assistance must be given. What "adequate assistance" means can only be determined by a factual analysis of the operating costs. In the meantime, the passing of this bill will tide us over.

I have listened with considerable interest, Mr. Speaker, to the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mrs. Shipley) in her attempt, shall I say, to steal the halo from the head of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) and put it on the head of the mining operators of this country. I was not able to follow the bewildering array of statistics that she paraded before this corner of the house, but I should like to point out one fact in defence of the hon. member for York South. I am quite sure he is able to take care of himself, but she mentioned a statement he made that the workers in the gold mining industry had never, at any time, received a fair share of the wealth they produce. She made certain comparisons with certain other industries. All I would say is that, so far as I can recall, the hon. member for York South did not say he considered the workers in these other industries had received their fair share of the wealth they had produced, either. Perhaps in inferring that he was suggesting the operators of gold mines were, to a greater degree, more greedy than the operators of some of our other industries, she was creating a slightly erroneous impression.
I was somewhat interested in her earlier remarks when she spoke of someone going around with a trowel and sealing off certain sections of the mine. Speaking as one old miner to another, I would suggest that there were one or two things she may have overlooked in her consideration of this particular aspect of the matter. Apparently she has never heard of the idea of blocking off reserves of ore or of a diamond drilling program which may serve to indicate where certain sources of rich ores may lie.
I am sorry, I did not say that.

That is just the point, Mr. Speaker, I said that was what she did not say. Perhaps the miners in Ontario are not as wise as the miners of British Columbia in certain mining techniques. To illustrate what I mean, I recall that back in the 1930's a certain large mine in British Columbia, which is known primarily as a producer of copper, found itself in a position where for a period of two years they were not able to sell a pound of copper. I am speaking only from memory now. This mine continued to operate on a somewhat reduced scale all during that period. They managed
Gold Mining
to do that because of the superior mining technique that we have in British Columbia.
They knew that in certain areas of that mine there were ores that had a considerable gold content. They concentrated their mining in those particular areas, and paid their operating costs out of the gold that was normally a minor incidental to their production. However, I am not going to attempt to go into a detailed analysis, as I said, of that array of statistics that was given to us.
I was quite interested in the remarks that were made by the member who spoke before the hon. member for Timiskaming. He gave us an interesting outline of some of the economic factors that exist today in the gold mining industry. As I sat listening to these two speakers, the main point that struck me was that they were on the horns of a dilemma. Since coming to this house I have all too often seen the members on that side in a similar dilemma. They are the victims of the sort of patchwork policy the present administration seems to be content to pursue in dealing with the various economic problems that arise in this country.
In referring to that, I would suggest that there is a limit to the number of patches you can put on anything. When you start putting patches on the patches, and then patches on the patches on the patches, you begin to get a sort of Joseph's coat of government policy such as we see developing now. This bill, like some of the other bills that have come before us in the short time I have been here, illustrates to me the dilemma in which the government is. Incidentally, of course, the members in the small opposition groups are in a dilemma also. If we do not support this measure, it is said, the gold miners are going to go hungry, and that is quite true. For that reason, we cannot do anything else but go along with this idea that assistance to the gold mines, under existing circumstances, is necessary. Sometimes when you listen to the array of statistics showing the moneys granted over a period of years you begin to ask yourself, how long is this going to continue? Are we going to extend this thing next year and the following year- for the next fifty years-or are we not? Why do we keep the gold mining industry operating in Canada, if it has to be subsidized? Those are questions that any thoughtful member must ask himself when a bill of this kind comes before the house.
I have to admit that some of my interest in and knowledge of the gold mining industry dates from the period referred to as the great depression; and I have wondered if possibly the government is continuing this measure, for the support of the gold mines, as a form

Gold Mining
of depression insurance. Because many of us can recall that in the days of the great depression there was one small sector of our economy in which there was no depression; and that was the gold mining industry: there was a boom there. Everyone connected with gold mining was prosperous, relatively speaking. The only difficulty was that perhaps only one in a hundred of the people who would have liked to get in on the gold mining industry were able to do so.
I have come to this point because, as I say, this is another example of the dilemma we find ourselves in. We had one not so long ago when we were discussing a measure concerning anti-dumping provisions for the protection of certain other industries in Canada. Then, reference was made recently to the dilemma in which the coal mining areas of the maritime provinces find themselves today. I felt that in view of all these facts it would be worth while for me to rise in the debate and once again draw attention to the point I brought out during the debate on unemployment.
As reported at page 2386 of Hansard for February 23, I said:
I suggest it is time to do something more than review our unemployment insurance plan. It is time for the government ... to launch a new insurance plan, one which I would call re-establishment insurance. This plan would cover those people the Acting Prime Minister has advised to go elsewhere to seek work. It would insure them against the loss of their homes, and against having to walk away and simply leave behind everything they have accumulated over a period of years. It would be a plan which would cover retraining these people in another industry.
I mention this because, if such a comprehensive plan were in existence, we might be able to view the present measure in an altogether different light. Under those circumstances we could proceed intelligently with an inquiry into the gold mining industry, as was suggested yesterday by the hon. member for York South. We could analyse the situation impartially, to ascertain whether the continuance of this industry for the next fifty years, under the present uneconomic conditions, would be warranted and in the national interest. We could decide whether we really need gold in our modern economy.
But because I know, as every other member knows, that if this measure is not passed the lives of thousands of people-I believe the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mrs. Shipley) gave the figure of 500,000 people- will be disrupted, and that many would suffer complete economic disaster, we have to continue to go along with this kind of patchwork measure.
When we think of this industry, and then think of the textile industry, and the possibility of the same sort of thing developing

in other industries, the necessity for some well-thought-out plan to take care of this situation becomes more and more apparent. That, Mr. Speaker, is my primary reason for taking part in this debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. George Prudham (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise now especially to thank those who have indicated their support of the bill, and would refer particularly to the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mrs. Shipley) and the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Dumas) for the wealth of information they have given the house this afternoon. I should like also to deal with a few statements made and questions asked by various members.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) and others have suggested that a commission should' be appointed to make an inquiry into the gold mining industry. I would remind hon. members that this parliament has no direct jurisdiction over the development of our natural resources. That comes within the constitutional rights of the provinces. They have the control of the administration and the development of resources within their own boundaries, and also labour regulations and the conditions obtaining within their jurisdictions.
I believe in all of the provinces facilities are available for collective bargaining. Any group of employees or any union has the privilege of entering into collective bargaining arrangements with management, and thus reach mutually satisfactory agreements. The suggestion has been made that we should look ahead' as far as fifty years. I do not think that is a reasonable suggestion. Indeed, I am sure it is not, when one considers that the actual development of our resources does not date back much more than fifty years. I believe any policy adopted by the government and parliament has to be flexible enough to meet changing conditions.
We think we have seen development in Canada in the last few years; in my opinion we have not seen anything yet. This country is just starting to move. Conditions as we know them today will be entirely different next year or the year after. I know my friends of the C.C.F. are dedicated to the socialization of our resources. But the people of Canada are not; otherwise we would have more C.C.F.'ers here.
Heaven forbid.
