The hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) referred to the number of people who would be disrupted if the gold mines were to go out of business. The hon. member for York South suggested that there would be hundreds of thousands and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni mentioned 500,000. Actually there are between 21,000 and 22,000-

I was quoting a figure
suggested by another hon. member.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
The actual number of
people working in the mines is somewhere between 21,000 and 22,000, but of course there would be their families and their communities dependent upon them. I admit that it would be a disaster if the gold mines had to close, but I question whether there would be actually hundreds of thousands of people directly involved in any such disaster.
The hon. member for York South suggested that two mines received a large proportion of the gold mining assistance paid. Two mines received approximately $1,300,000 of the $10,359,053.90, or about 12.5 per cent of the total amount paid. However, they produced
Gold Mining
511,670 ounces out of a total of 2,638,032 ounces, or about 19 per cent of the gold produced during that period.
As I said in my remarks the other day, the gold mining industry as a whole, including labour and management, has responded to the challenge. Their costs of production have been reduced progressively since the war and in my opinion they have done a good job in helping themselves. As I have said before in this house, when an industry shows that it is doing everything to help itself, that is a good reason why the government should consider extending aid over a difficult period. I have told the coal miners that and I believe the same rule applies to the gold mines. When they show that they have gone all-out to help themselves, I think there is justification for government aid in an emergency.
This is not a patchwork policy, as the last speaker has suggested. As the title of the act implies, this aid is to meet an emergency which we hope will be of short duration. The chief reason for extending emergency gold mining assistance last year and this year was and is to compensate to some extent for the loss to the mine because of the appreciation of the value of the Canadian dollar in terms of United States funds. That situation fluctuates from time to time and we do not know how long our dollar will remain in that favourable position. If it should change there would be less need for aid to the gold mines.
The hon. member for York South asked whether the mines are making excessive profits. I think the fact that 40 mines have closed since the beginning of emergency gold mining assistance with only 27 new mines being opened-some 13 of those new mines have since closed-is pretty good evidence that no excessive profits are being made.
I believe that many people overlook the fact that the development of our mining resources is a co-operative effort. It requires the co-operation of a number of groups of people. One group that is often overlooked is the investors. The mining industry at best is a depleting industry. When you remove ore from the ground it will never be replaced. If we are to develop our mining industry we must attract risk capital by showing a reasonable chance to make a profit. When the flow of risk capital dries up, your industry dies just as surely as if the men stopped working. With all the mines closing last year-there were 6 gold mines closed with no new ones being opened-I think that is the best evidence that excessive profits are not being made.

Gold Mining
I should like to answer a query by the hon. member for York South about the formula used as reported in a sessional paper in regard to the Hollinger mine. Even for the experts this gold mining assistance formula is not simple in operation and I do not wonder that my hon. friend is confused. I have had difficulty in following it in particular instances. The explanation I have for the point which he mentioned is that to get the calculation for the assistance payable per ounce of gold produced a mine is considered as being in operation during the whole year. The same result would be obtained by prorating the base year for a similar period for which operations were not suspended and using the actual production. The method of calculation is set out in the regulations and I want to assure my hon. friend once again that it gives no advantage to a mine during a period of a strike.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Applewhaite in the chair.
On clause 1-Application of act to 1951, 1952, 1953 and 1954.

Mr. Chairman, before we pass clause 1 I would like to say a few words. I regret very much the minister has taken the position that because the federal government has no jurisdiction over natural resources he does not choose to consider the setting up of a committee or commission to study the gold mining industry. I had hoped that, in view of the fact that the government of Canada was involved to the extent of well over $10 million per year in the form of subsidies, that would give the government an interest in such an inquiry. In fact, I believe such an inquiry would be beneficial both to the industry and to the miners and the mine owners.
That is evidenced by the honest difference of opinion regarding the status of the gold mining industry at the present time. I am quite sure that the hon. member for Timiska-ming is just as honest and serious in her views regarding the status of the gold mines as I am in mine. The difference of opinion which exists between us is not only reflected in this house but is to be found between employees and employers and their respective organizations. It is to be found as between the chairmen of conciliation boards and representatives of the miners and mine owners.
But I am confident that if the premier of Ontario carries out, as I hope he will, his agreement with the steel workers union to establish a provincial committee on a very high level for the purpose of undertaking a

thorough factual investigation of the gold mining industry, and if he will invite federal representation on that committee, and the federal government agrees to be represented there, nothing but good can result from such an investigation.
I was, of course, very interested in some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Timiskaming and I would like to congratulate her on the fighting attitude which she has adopted in the interests of those who sent her to parliament. I am quite sure her efforts will be appreciated by her supporters. I would simply say to her that I would be very happy at any time to set forth my point of view compared with hers at a public meeting in her own home town of Kirkland Lake any time she chooses to arrange such a meeting. I will be quite happy to allow the miners of that town to decide which point of view is correct.
It sounds like suicide.

I was, of course, amused by her statement that miners did not go around with trowels covering up gold nuggets here and there. I had hoped that the hon. member for Timiskaming was much more conversant with mining operations, and knew that gold from northern Ontario is not dug out in nuggets, but is saturated through tons of ore brought into the mill. Permit me to inform her that I doubt if there is very much about gold mining she can teach me. There is no process in gold mining operations, from mucking underground to refining, in which I have not participated at some time, so that I know something of what can be done by way of sealing off high-grade ore bodies when that becomes advantageous.
Would the hon. member permit a question? I wonder if he would mind stating when he last worked in a gold mine?

Quite frankly, Mr. Chairman, miners who are engaged in this kind of work and doing diamond drilling in the mines informed me no later than a few months ago that some mines at least are sealing off high-grade ore.
That does not answer my question.
Answer.
I am not saying-
I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, but the hon. member is not answering my question.
I am not going to give the hon. member the names of the individual miners-
My question was, how long ago did you work in a mine?
It was some time ago, Mr. Chairman.
But how long ago?
I have visited these mines regularly-
How long ago did you work in a mine?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: The hon. member has the protection of the House of Commons and I would ask him to name one mine which does as he suggests. I do not suppose he would dare to do so outside the house.

I do not care to give the names of the individual miners who gave me that information. The minister, for example, must know that McIntyre has reserves today which are probably of a higher grade and more extensive than this mine has ever had over the years.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Would the hon. member like to have the assay figures of the ore they have milled over the years?
I am simply asking the minister to make certain that mines are not running undue quantities of low-grade ore through their mills-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: You said they were.

-and salting it down with a small percentage of high-grade ore in order to mill much of their ore, which would otherwise be uneconomic, because of this subsidy. I am simply asking the minister and his department to make quite certain that is not being done. I realize there is always a question of just what policy will be in the best interests of the future life of the mine, and the future interests of the country, and just to what extent mines should be encouraged to continue uneconomic production. However, these are matters which, I suggest, a commission of investigation should be able to determine.
I am not surprised that mines pay more out in wages than they receive in subsidy, but I do not think it was ever the intention of the government that the subsidies they pay should cover the whole cost of wages. Nor am I surprised that there has been an increase in wages since 1947. Miners' wages were pretty low at the end of the war. Gold mining wages were fairly low at the end of the war. The fact still remains that, according to the dominion bureau of statistics, the average annual wage of gold miners in Canada was $1,343 as of June 1, 1953. The average annual wage of base metal miners across Canada on that same date, according
Gold Mining
to the dominion bureau of statistics, was $1,701. Therefore, notwithstanding any increases and notwithstanding subsidies, up until last June the gold miners were still far behind base metal miners in the matter of wages received. If gold mining is not profitable and if the mines cannot afford to pay to miners wages that are equivalent to those paid in, let us say, base metal mining or comparable industry, then the responsibility for making up that deficit must of necessity, I think, fall upon the country at large and not upon a particular group of employees.
If what the mine owners say is true and if the present subsidies are not large enough to enable them to pay to gold miners wages equivalent to those paid in base metal mining, it is possible that the subsidy should be increased. I do not know. But certainly if the mine owners' claims are true and if they cannot afford to pay the people in the gold mining industry as well as miners in the base metal industry are paid, then something should be done to make that possible. It is not fair to ask these miners to bear the loss incurred by the fact that the mine operators are operating an industry where the costs continue to rise and where the price of their product is fixed by governments. I am not quarrelling with the act or with the necessity for it. What I am asking is that there should be a thorough investigation of this industry. If these subsidies are not large enough, they should be increased. Certainly the miners should not be left in the position they are in today.
I am happy to hear the hon. member for Timiskaming defending the mine owners for their communities' support. I have heard municipal authorities complain that these gold mines were not bearing their share of municipal taxation. I am quite sure that it will be encouraging to know that the hon. member for Timiskaming, who has a great wealth of experience in municipal affairs, views their support with such a high degree of admiration.
In view of the very fact that under this act, the minister tells us, forty mines have been forced to close and so few mines have come into operation, and the fact that, of necessity, under the present act the larger producers of gold are getting the larger share of the subsidy, is it not worth considering whether or not this act is doing the job that it was intended to do, namely, that of helping some of the smaller mines? Is it rendering to the smaller mines-those that are operating at high cost-the assistance that it was originally intended it should render? Those are questions that I think we should consider. I greatly regret that the minister

Gold Mining
undertakes to shelve the whole matter by accepting the excuse that the federal government has no jurisdiction over natural resources.
I just wanted to ask the minister a couple of questions. I do not want to interrupt the train of argument. If the minister wants to reply now, I can wait.

And for the first nine months of last year the same recovery per ton was shown, namely [DOT]280. The average for the whole period was [DOT]290. If the grade had been increased last year to -290, McIntyre mines would receive $12,079.02 less in emergency gold mining assistance. An increase in production of 5,588 ounces of gold would have been valued at $195,582.83; that is at $35 an ounce. If, on the other hand, the grade had been lowered by -01 ounce per ton, McIntyre mines would receive $9,634.06 more in assistance. The decrease, however, would represent a decrease from sales of gold of $206,280.16.
This shows very clearly that it would be unprofitable to lower the grade of ore unless

it was necessary to do so on account of conditions in the mine. You just cannot win by low grading or hoping to collect on the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. As the grade of ore decreases the number of ounces decreases. You have the two factors, the rate of assistance applied to the number of eligible ounces. It is not possible to beat this provision. I hope the figures I have taken the time to put on the record will prove conclusively to my hon. friend that this is so. In so far as we can tell

and we are very confident-no one could beat the act, even if they wanted to, and we are confident on the basis of our inspection services that nobody is trying to.
I want to thank the minister for putting these figures on the record. I am quite sure they will help to clarify a situation about which there is a great deal of dispute.

I want to say something in answer to the same argument because I think it must be dealt with now. First of all may I say, in the somewhat more robust language of the north, that the hon. member for Timiskaming made a damn fine speech this afternoon. McIntyre mine has been referred to. I have been underground in McIntyre many times. Some years ago McIntyre discovered what is known as the twenty-five vein system. It is to the north of the property. It is a nearly vertical vein structure of quite high grade. It runs about an ounce per ton which is about four times the average grade at the mine.
As the hon. member for Timiskaming said, the ideal is to have a mill feed of constant grade running to the mill. The situation at McIntyre is that in the old Pearl lake porphyry area and the other older parts of the mine the grade may run from -15 to [DOT]2, perhaps even less than -15. This ore is mixed with a proportion from the twenty-five vein system area to bring the average grade up to what the minister said, about -29 ounces per ton.
So far as increased costs are concerned, let me take the case of Kerr-Addison. At the present time Kerr-Addison is probably the greatest gold mine in Canada and North America. Quite conceivably it may become the greatest gold mine in the world. It has a wonderful deposit of ore. Years ago before the war they cut off mining or hoisting or breaking ore when they got below -06 ounces per ton. As costs rose they stopped breaking at -07 and as they rose further at [DOT]08, -09 until now I believe any rock containing less than one-tenth of an ounce is considered waste rock.

The quantity of ore between -06 ounces per ton and -1 ounces per ton runs to many hundreds of thousands of tons, and many thousands of dollars' worth of gold is lost to Canada and to the national wealth of the country for all time. That is an example of what increased costs are doing so far as the destruction of our national wealth is concerned.
With regard to the question of sealing off, in one, maybe two, and possibly three cases that I know of an extremely high grade section was discovered and sealed oft. I think the highest grade section was discovered some years ago at the O'Brien mine in the Cadillac area. I have forgotten what it ran, but it was 20, 30 or perhaps even 50 ounces per ton over a very short distance and a very small ore chute. I am not sure how big it was but I saw the ore in place and it was just like looking at the national mint. It was a very beautiful sight. But it was a very small occurrence and to safeguard that very high grade deposit the stope was barred and locked to prevent high grading. That was some years ago.
There may have been one or two other cases. Siscoe had some high grade and there may have been other cases where, a small chute of tremendously high grade ore having been discovered, it was wired off for a temporary period simply and solely to prevent high grading until such time as the ore could be mined. Incidentally, that was a long time before the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act came into force and had nothing to do with sealing off high grade ore in order to mine low grade ore. What the hon. member for Timiskaming has said is absolutely correct. It is nothing short of ridiculous to think that any mine would seal off high grade today.

I should like to ask the minister a couple of questions. Before doing so, I should like to say that along with my colleagues I support entirely the continuation of this act for another year. However, in view of comments which I read in the press this morning I should like to ask the minister to clear up one matter. As I understood those comments, they certainly gave rise to the suggestion at any rate that the minister had said that the government would only continue this assistance for one year, and it was represented that it was almost their intention to discontinue it after a further year. On referring to page 3030 of Hansard of March 16 I find the minister said:
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, may I say that in presenting this resolution for an extension of assistance for the year 1954 it is the government's hope that this extension will enable the gold mines to continue their operations so that eventually they may be able to carry on without this emergency
Gold Mining
assistance. It has always been the government's intention that this assistance should be only of a temporary nature.
As I read that statement, it is quite different from the conclusion I formed after reading the press comment this morning, and I should like the minister to clear up the matter for me. While appreciating the desire, which I think we all share, that as soon as possible the gold mining industry may be restored to a healthy state so that this assistance will not be necessary, is it a fact that the government has not placed any time limit on the period for which they are prepared to continue the assistance but are merely hoping they will be able to discontinue it as soon as possible?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: I stated the government's case quite clearly yesterday, as my hon. friend indicated when he read from Hansard. We are asking for an extension of this act to the end of this year only. We hope it is the last time it will be necessary to extend it. However, as has been the case ever since 1948, we expect to review the situation at the end of the year. I am not holding out any hope it will be extended another year. I certainly hope it will not be necessary.

No more significance should be attached to the fact that it is only continued for one year on this occasion than to the fact that previous extensions have also been one-year extensions. Would that be a correct statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: It is up to my hon. friend as to what he infers from what I have said. When the original bill and the extensions have been before the house, we have always said that the measure was designed to meet an emergency. When that emergency is over, there will be no more need for this assistance.

There is another point about which I should like to ask the minister. Is it a fact that under this legislation there is no compensation to the mines for the fact that the price of their product has decreased?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, that is the purpose of this bill, to compensate the mines for the fixed price which they receive for their products.

I am sorry I did not make my question clear. There is no additional compensation under the legislation now being continued to take care of the fact that the price of gold has decreased within the last year. The hon. member for York West and the minister both placed on Hansard last night the price of gold during the current year, which appears to be $33.79 per ounce as of March 6. This represents a decline over the last year or two as a result of the increase

Gold Mining
in the value of the Canadian dollar in terms of the United States dollar. I am asking for confirmation of the fact that there is no increased measure of assistance now being offered to make up for the fact that within the last twelve months there has been a further decline in the price of gold.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Two years ago there was an amendment to the act to provide additional assistance. The need for the additional assistance at that time was brought about by a decline in the price of gold. It depends upon how a mine owner likes to assess his problem, whether he thinks the price of gold is too low or his costs are too high. This assistance is designed to assist the mines.

I think we are getting at the point now. The minister says the amendment was introduced two years ago. Is it not a fact that the price of the Canadian dollar, in terms of the United States dollar, has increased further since that amendment was made two years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: The average mint price in terms of Canadian dollars was, in 1942 to 1945, $38.50; in 1946, $36.75; in 1947-48, $35; in 1949, $36; in 1950, $38.05; 1951, $36.85. On February 20 of this year it was $33.81 and on March 6 last it was $33.79. The price has been fluctuating. It is down from 1951, but we have increased the assistance since that time.

The assistance was increased in 1952, and the figures the minister has placed on the record indicate there has been a further decline from 1952 to the present time. He did not put on the record the figures for 1952. In 1951, the price was $36.85. I think it is fair to point out that there has been an increase in the price of the Canadian dollar since that amendment two years ago, which would produce a corresponding decrease in the price of gold to the Canadian producer.
The reason I wanted to make that point was that it seemed to me the government should perhaps contemplate some further measure of assistance to take care of the continuing decrease in the price of Canadian gold. Two years ago 1 did not hear anyone seriously suggest that the measure of assistance being provided, even under the amendment, was overly generous. I think the government's attitude has been to provide sufficient assistance to enable the mines to continue in operation. If two years ago the assistance then provided was no more than enough to enable them to continue in operation, and the price of gold to the Canadian producer has declined since, does it not follow the government should be revising the

scale of assistance? I think it does. I should like to know from the minister what representations have been made on that point, and what consideration, if any, has been given to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: We do not propose any increase for this year.

In conclusion, I should like to lay before the minister the suggestion that if the gold mines and those engaged in the gold mining industry are to be enabled to carry on on a comparable standard with the rest of the people, and particularly with those engaged in other forms of mining activity, then it seems to me we should be making some adjustment in the scale of assistance to compensate for the further decline in the price of gold since the last adjustment was made. I strongly urge the minister and his department to undertake a review in that connection, to see if they would not agree with me as to the necessity for an adjustment.
I have in mind the two quite large gold mines in my own constituency, the Pioneer and Bralorne mines. They are, as most mines are, in remote areas. There is no other town except the mine, and there are no other facilities there. They are purely mining towns. The cost of everything the people living there have to buy is high because it is a small community and supplies must be trucked in over some 47 miles of extremely mountainous road. These men are faced with the impossibility of any adjustment in their wage rates as a result of the limits on the assistance provided, and yet they are faced with a cost of living much higher than in most other communities in the country.
If two years ago the assistance was no more than enough to enable the mines to continue in operation, and the price of gold has declined since but the assistance has not increased, then it seems to me that forms a strong argument in favour of a review so that those engaged in the gold mining industry can maintain a standard comparable with those in other forms of activity.

I heard with considerable interest the minister's statement a moment ago, that he looked forward to the possibility that it might not be necessary a year hence to continue this form of assistance to the gold mining industry. On what grounds does he base that hope?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, as I said in my opening remarks on the resolution, the industry has responded to the challenge, it has decreased its cost of producing an ounce of gold, and has produced more per man-day. To a large extent that has been brought about by improved methods

and increased mechanization. I do not think even the mines themselves would suggest that they have done everything or that there is no room tor improvement, as new techniques develop. I think that is the way the problem should be solved, rather than by increasing the government subsidy every time there is increased disparity between costs and sale price.

I was hoping the minister would say something about the other factor which, I suggest, is much more important than either of the factors he mentioned. I refer to the price of gold. Has the minister any grounds for hoping that within the next year we may look for an increase in the price of gold?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: I have no grounds for that hope. I am satisfied this government is doing everything possible to influence an increase in the price of gold. The hon. member for York West suggested that we should lead the world by increasing the price. Well, I do not believe anyone who gives the matter serious consideration would advocate that we increase the price of gold to, let us say, $50, and be prepared to accept all the gold that would flow into this country from all parts of the world. Fifteen million people certainly cannot become the bankers for the world. We hope that the United States some day will see fit to raise the price of gold, but we do not know when that might be; and there presently is no indication of it.

Clause agreed to.
Bill reported.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, March 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chevrier for the second reading of Bill No. 374, to control export and import of strategic materials.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter of governmental control over exports and imports is no stranger to the house. Export control over materials was established in 1941 under the War Measures Act, and we have had it in one form or another ever since.
The Export and Import Permits Act was first enacted by parliament in 1947. It has since come before the house, through amending measures, in 1948, in the second session of 1949 and in 1951. When the measure was 83276-196
Export and Import Permits Act first introduced it was placed in the category of measures to carry forward controls that had existed during the war. Indeed, sir, clause 14 of the bill then introduced, as it appears in chapter 17 of the statutes of 1947, contained this provision:
This act shall come into force upon the expiration of the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945, and shall expire sixty days from the commencement of the first session of parliament commencing in the year one thousand nine hundred and forty-eight.
It was put before the house at that time as legislation to deal with a type of emergency which was thought still to exist in 1947 and which, in the period when the War Measures Act had ceased to be in effect, had been carried forward under the authority of the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945.
In the various extensions of this measure, it has always been put before the house as a measure of limited duration. I have indicated that when it was introduced in 1947 it was to expire in 1948. In 1948 an amendment was introduced which extended the period of life of the measure to March 31, 1950. In the second session of 1949 the life of the measure was extended to July 31, 1951. Then at the 1951 session the life of the measure was extended to July 31, 1954. And, unless extended in some form at this present session, it will expire on that date.
I have mentioned that the measure was introduced as one designed to cope with an emergency. The emergency, as described by the minister who introduced the measure on February 18, 1947, is of a nature comparable in no way, I suggest, with the conditions of today. The Hon. Mr. MacKinnon, at page 568 of Hansard for that date, referred to the main purpose of export control in these words:
While the main purpose of the export control is to ensure adequate supply in Canada, the export controls are also necessary to enable us to carry out Canada's commitments in connection with those foodstuffs which are in world short supply and which, by common agreement of the united nations, must be formally allocated to ensure an equitable distribution.
And then he made mention of a third form of control, or a third purpose of control, and said this:
A third type of control which is envisaged by this measure is that relating to the movement of arms, munitions and war materials and supplies.
I am sure I do not need to dwell at length upon the radical change in the situation as between February 18, 1947, and today, March 17, 1954-the 17th of Ireland.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CONTROL OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext:
There is no longer any scarcity of goods in Canada which must be assisted
3094	HOUSE OF
E&port and Import Permits Act by control over exports, nor is Canada lacking the foodstuffs or other materials necessary to fulfil international agreements at this time. The third type of control mentioned by the Hon. Mr. MacKinnon in the extract from which I have just read is one that is much more in our minds today.
When the measure came before the house in 1947 it was proposed on behalf of the official opposition by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) that the whole subject should be carefully reviewed in the banking and commerce committee. His suggestion was accepted on behalf of the government by the Hon. Mr. MacKinnon, then minister of trade and commerce. It will be remembered that a very useful review of the whole structure of export and import control was carried out in the banking and commerce committee.
When the measure was reported back to the house I think there was general recognition of the fact that the reference to the banking and commerce committee had been a highly useful procedure. Mr. Speaker, I am again suggesting to the house that an equally useful purpose would now be served by the reference of this measure to the banking and commerce committee. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) is not present with us today, being absent in Washington on official duties attending an important international conference, but I am laying that suggestion before the government and before the house as one which I think will facilitate the business of the house and also contribute considerably to an adequate review of this control structure.
When the measure was under debate at that time the hon. member for Greenwood, speaking for the official opposition, drew attention to three fundamental considerations that should weigh with the house in reference to a measure of this kind. I suggest that those observations are equally valid today. First of all, he expressed a dislike of controls as the kind of interference which in ordinary circumstances tampers with the free flow of sound economic forces. In the second place, he expressed a dislike of government by order in council. Every measure of this kind inevitably involves the conferring of power upon the governor in council virtually to legislate by that means. That objection is as strong today as it was in 1947, or stronger. The third consideration which he drew to the attention of the house at that time was the danger of placing in the hands of the government a weapon or power which could be used to create monopoly or to impose a discrimination between different Canadian exporters or different Canadian 

importers. When the measure was brought back to the house after review in the banking and commerce committee an attempt was made to control the date of expiration of the measure more effectively, but that amendment of the hon. member for Greenwood was defeated.
Those who sat in the last parliament will recall that when this measure came before the house in 1951 there were two forms of extension involved. One was the extension in point of time; the other was an extension in the type of control contemplated by it.
So far as the extension in point of time is concerned, it was the proposal of the government at that time that the extension should be for a period of five years to July 31, 1956. I will say this for the work done on the measure in the other place that that extension was reduced to three years. A somewhat similar reduction in the length of the extension had been proposed in this house, but it was rejected by the government. Mr. Speaker, I should have thought it necessary with respect to a measure of this kind, which can only justify its existence on the basis of the existence of an emergency, that the house should insist that an opportunity would be afforded to it for a periodical review and that there should be nothing in the nature of a long or indefinite extension of time. The three-year extension did carry and we are now faced with the conclusion of that three-year period.
The other form of extension made by the 1951 amendment was in the nature of the control. Up until that time the control had been upon a commodity basis. In 1951 control on a country basis was added. That was a very important extension. The reason was quite obvious. It was in the period following the outbreak of communist aggression in Korea and no objection was taken to that particular type of extension under the emergent conditions which were then described as existing.
In this 1954 session we are invited to consider the replacement of the Export and Import Permits Act. The measure now under debate contemplates the repeal of the existing legislation and its replacement by a new Export and Import Permits Act, which presumably in some respects will carry further the broad structure of controls existing under the present legislation.
I think that this is a measure of high importance. It brings us face to face with many far-reaching questions in relation to trade policy, particularly in the type of world we are living in where a cold war still is being waged and where a hot war

is being fought in certain unhappy parts of Asia. It is with that background that we approach this measure.
It is fair to ask at once: What is the extent of the use made by the government of the powers conferred upon it under the existing legislation? It is proper to answer that the use of the power has been quite extensive with respect to export but very limited with respect to import. May I give the house the details of the permits issued in the past four years:

The export permits outnumber the import permits by fifty times. The question then naturally arises: What is the necessity for import control? I submit that that is a matter which should have serious consideration, which should have a more serious and extended study than is possible in the house or in the committee of the whole. It is a subject that ought to engage the attention of a committee like the banking and commerce committee.
One example of the use of this power of limiting exports comes to mind at once, and I refer to the limitation announced in the house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on December 14, 1953, with respect to the export to the United States of Canadian oats. This is in truth an example of the control of exports which has no relation to strategic materials, which has no relation to arms, which has no relation to war materials or munitions, but which is used as an instrument of trade policy.
I ask the house to consider whether this is the type of use of a controlling power which the house approves. At that time it was announced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce as a government decision that effective at midnight December 10, 1953, and continuing until midnight September 30, 1954, the Canadian government had undertaken to limit the shipment of Canadian oats to the United States to 23 million bushels. The reason given was that the United States executive had asked that this measure be taken by the Canadian government in order that the United States government might not be faced with what was then an imminent breach of the general agreement on tariffs and trade by the United States congress.
It may have been very accommodating to the government of the United States that the government of Canada should come to its 83276-196i
Export and Import Permits Act rescue in this situation and impose this limitation on the export of Canadian oats to the United States. But what are the hard realities of the situation? The fact is that the United States congress deliberately violated the general agreement on tariffs and trade in 1952 with respect to the importation into that country of certain dairy products. In 1953 they again violated the general agreement on tariffs and trade, and again with reference to certain dairy products, by the extension of the products to which certain prohibitory legislation applied, and now congress, at the end of 1953, apparently is on the point of again violating the general agreement on tariffs and trade by applying restrictions on the importation of Canadian oats into that country. The Canadian government rises to the occasion and accommodates the executive of the United States by imposing these restrictions upon the export of Canadian oats to the United States so that, apparently, the United States congress will not be put in the position of violating, as it has in fact and in spirit, the general agreement on tariffs and trade. I for one, Mr. Speaker, fail to understand why it became the duty of the Canadian government, the considered responsibility of the Canadian government, to take that action at that time.
If the United States congress at the expense of the Canadian farmer is determined to violate the spirit and the letter of the general agreement on tariffs and trade- a shocking violation of good faith in a world in which violations of good faith on the part of nations in the west are critically examined by those in the world who are not our friends -then I believe that that responsibility should be allowed to rest squarely where it belongs, namely on the United States congress as the violator of the agreement. The Canadian government should not step forward and impose limitations upon the export of Canadian grain to accommodate the United States congress.
I now pass on, Mr. Speaker, to a consideration of the effect of this measure in relation to a subject of even wider significance. This measure before us is described as "an act respecting the export and import of strategic and other goods". Let us dwell for a moment on the importance of that word "strategic". The word itself, of course, is not defined in the bill. Its exact import may be a matter of debate in certain particulars, but its significance is, I believe, beyond question. We are thinking here in terms of ensuring that materials which would be of assistance to aggressors in the world today are not permitted to fall into the hands of those aggressors, either by direct export of such
3096	HOUSE OF
Export and Import Permits Act goods to those aggressors, or by export elsewhere under such circumstances that they will by indirect methods eventually fall into the hands of those would-be aggressors.
This, Mr. Speaker, raises some very far-reaching and searching questions as to trade policy, and as to the relationship of trade considerations to the whole broad question of the peace of the world. In examining the figures on trade with nations which lie behind the iron curtain one finds some rather interesting facts. First of all, let us look at our export trade with Russia. In 1952 we exported to Russia a total of $421 worth of goods, in 1953 a total of $478 worth of goods. The records indicate that these goods exported were: settlers' effects, books, liquor, and donations. Our trade with China shows some rather interesting figures also. In 1952 we exported to China goods to the value of $1,155,524, and in 1953 the total was nil. If one looks at trade with Hong Kong as reflecting something of the trade we formerly did with China it will be seen that in 1952 our export trade to Hong Kong amounted to a total of $9,581,937, and in 1953 $8,999,606. I am not going to deal with the other countries which lie behind the iron curtain but I will mention one with which we used to do a rather important trade, namely Czechoslovakia. Our exports to Czechoslovakia in 1952 were only $366,229. In 1953 they have fallen further to a total of only $122,691.
It is worth noting, Mr. Speaker, that since 1951, under the powers conferred by the existing legislation, the government has enlarged the number of countries with which trade is proscribed except on an export permit basis. The 1953 report of the Department of Trade and Commerce in relation to this measure shows that since January 13, 1953, the number of proscribed countries, to which goods are not permitted to move except under permit, are the following: North Korea, Hong Kong, China, Macao, Manchuria, Mongolia, Sinkiang, Tibet, Albania, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, Estonia, the Russian occupied zone of Germany, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Danzig, Roumania, the Ukraine, and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. That represents a very much enlarged list of countries as compared with the previous list of proscribed countries since the power to control export by countries was conferred upon the governor in council in 1951. I am quite sure, Mr. Speaker, that no one in this house questions the wisdom of extending the prohibition to all these countries, except on the permit basis.
